title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 69 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 444–446 (Night 69, continuing directly from nights-68), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 69 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. Sharkān, learning that the girl he bought is his own sister, resolves to hide the shame by marrying her to his chief chamberlain, and names her daughter Quḍiya-fa-kān. Then a courier brings a letter from King ʿUmar demanding the tribute of Damascus and the girl, on account of a learned old woman and her five young scholars from the lands of Rome. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ التَّاسِعَةُ وَالسِّتُّونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-tāsiʿatu wa-al-sittūna
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the ninth and the sixty,
sentences.i: And when it was the sixty-ninth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ شَرْكَانَ لَمَّا سَمِعَ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ ارْتَجَفَ قَلْبُهُ وَاصْفَرَّ لَوْنُهُ وَلَحِقَهُ الِارْتِعَاشُ وَأَطْرَقَ بِرَأْسِهِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ وَعَرَفَ أَنَّهَا أُخْتُهُ مِنْ أَبِيهِ فَغَابَ عَنِ الدُّنْيَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Sharkāna lammā samiʿa hādhā al-kalāma irtajafa qalbuhu wa-iṣfarra lawnuhu wa-laḥiqahu al-irtiʿāshu wa-aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi ilā al-arḍi wa-ʿarafa annahā ukhtuhu min abīhi fa-ghāba ʿani al-dunyā
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the fortunate, that Sharkān, when he heard this speech, his heart shook and his colour yellowed, and trembling overtook him, and he bowed with his head to the ground, and he knew that she was his sister from his father, and he was absent from the world.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Sharkān heard these words, his heart shook and his colour turned pale, a trembling seized him, and he bowed his head to the ground. He knew that she was his sister by his father, and he lost consciousness of the world.
sentences.n: The print has الارتعاس, a misprint for الارتعاش, corrected here. The print runs السعيد and أن together (al-saʿīdu anna). In the print the name is شركان (Sharkān).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَفَاقَ صَارَ يَتَعَجَّبُ وَلَكِنَّهُ لَمْ يُعَرِّفْهَا بِنَفْسِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā afāqa ṣāra yataʿajjabu wa-lakinnahu lam yuʿarrifhā bi-nafsihi
sentences.l: And when he came to, he became wondering, but he did not make-her-know with his self.
sentences.i: When he came to himself he was amazed, but he did not make himself known to her.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا يَاسَيِّدَتِي هَلْ أَنْتِ بِنْتُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā yā sayyidatī hal anti bintu al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni
sentences.l: And he said to her: O my lady, are you daughter-of the king ʿUmar son-of al-Nuʿmān?
sentences.i: And he said to her, “My lady, are you the daughter of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān?”

sentences.t: قَالَتْ نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: qālat naʿam
sentences.l: She said: Yes.
sentences.i: She said, “Yes.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا احْكِي لِي عَنْ سَبَبِ فِرَاقِكِ لِوَالِدِكِ وَبَيْعِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā iḥkī lī ʿan sababi firāqiki li-wālidiki wa-bayʿiki
sentences.l: And he said to her: Tell to me about the cause-of your parting for your father, and your selling.
sentences.i: He said to her, “Tell me why you parted from your father, and how you came to be sold.”

sentences.t: فَحَكَتْ لَهُ عَلَى مَا جَمِيعَ وَقَعَ لَهَا مِنَ الْأَوَّلِ إِلَى الْآخِرِ وَأَخْبَرَتْهُ أَنَّهَا تَرَكَتْ أَخَاهَا مَرِيضًا فِي بَيْتِ الْمَقْدِسِ وَأَخْبَرَتْهُ بِاخْتِطَافِ الْبَدَوِيِّ لَهَا وَبَيْعِهِ إِيَّاهَا لِلتَّاجِرِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥakat lahu ʿalā mā jamīʿa waqaʿa lahā min al-awwali ilā al-ākhiri wa-akhbaratuhu annahā tarakat akhāhā marīḍan fī bayti al-maqdisi wa-akhbaratuhu bi-ikhtiṭāfi al-badawiyyi lahā wa-bayʿihi iyyāhā li-al-tājiri
sentences.l: And she told him, upon what all had befallen her, from the first to the last, and she informed him that she had left her brother sick in the House of the Holy-Place, and informed him of the Bedouin's seizing of her and his selling of her to the merchant.
sentences.i: She told him everything that had befallen her, from first to last. She told him that she had left her brother ill in Jerusalem, and told him how the Bedouin had seized her and sold her to the merchant.
sentences.n: The print has جميع (“all”) misplaced after على ما; it is read as على جميع ما وقع “all that befell”. Bayt al-Maqdis, “the Holy House”, is Jerusalem.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ شَرْكَانُ ذَلِكَ الْكَلَامَ تَحَقَّقَ أَنَّهَا أُخْتُهُ مِنْ أَبِيهِ وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ كَيْفَ أَتَزَوَّجُ بِأُخْتِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Sharkānu dhālika al-kalāma taḥaqqaqa annahā ukhtuhu min abīhi wa-qāla fī nafsihi kayfa atazawwaju bi-ukhtī
sentences.l: And when Sharkān heard that speech, he made-certain that she was his sister from his father, and he said in his self: How shall I marry with my sister?
sentences.i: When Sharkān heard this, he was certain that she was his sister by his father, and he said to himself, “How can I marry my own sister?”

sentences.t: وَلَكِنْ وَاللَّهِ لَابُدَّأَنْ أُزَوِّجَهَا لِوَاحِدٍ مِنْ حُجَّابِي وَإِذَا ظَهَرَ أَمْرٌ أَدَّعِي أَنَّنِي طَلَّقْتُهَا قَبْلَ الدُّخُولِ وَزَوَّجْتُهَا بِالْحَاجِبِ الْكَبِيرِ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin wa-allāhi lā budda an uzawwijahā li-wāḥidin min ḥujjābī wa-idhā ẓahara amrun addaʿī annanī ṭallaqtuhā qabla al-dukhūli wa-zawwajtuhā bi-al-ḥājibi al-kabīri
sentences.l: But by God, there is no avoiding that I marry-her-off to one of my chamberlains, and if a matter appears, I shall claim that I divorced her before the going-in and married her to the great chamberlain.
sentences.i: But by God, I must marry her off to one of my chamberlains; and if the matter comes to light, I shall claim that I divorced her before the marriage was consummated and gave her in marriage to the chief chamberlain.
sentences.n: قبل الدخول, “before the going-in”, is the standard phrase for before consummation of a marriage.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَفَعَ رَأْسَهُ وَتَأَسَّفَ وَقَالَ يَانُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ أَنْتِ أُخْتِي حَقِيقَةً وَأَنَا أَقُولُ أَسْتَغْفِرُ اللَّهَ مِنْ هَذَا الذَّنْبِ الَّذِي وَقَعْنَا فِيهِ فَإِنِّي أَنَا شَرْكَانُ ابْنُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَبْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma rafaʿa raʾsahu wa-taʾassafa wa-qāla yā Nuzhata al-zamāni anti ukhtī ḥaqīqatan wa-anā aqūlu astaghfiru Allāha min hādhā al-dhanbi alladhī waqaʿnā fīhi fa-innī anā Sharkānu ibnu al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni
sentences.l: Then he raised his head and grieved, and said: O Nuzhat of-the-time, you are my sister in truth, and I say: I ask God's forgiveness for this sin which we have fallen into. For I, I am Sharkān, son-of the king ʿUmar son-of al-Nuʿmān.
sentences.i: Then he raised his head, sorrowing, and said, “Nuzhat al-Zamān, you are truly my sister, and I say, I ask God's forgiveness for this sin we have fallen into. For I am Sharkān, son of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān.”

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَحَقَّقَتْهُ فَلَمَّا عَرَفَتْهُ غَابَتْ عَنْ صَوَابِهَا وَبَكَتْ وَلَطَمَتْ وَجْهَهَا وَقَالَتْ لَاحَوْلَ وَلَاقُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ قَدْ وَقَعْنَا فِي ذَنْبٍ عَظِيمٍ مَاذَا يَكُونُ الْعَمَلُ وَمَا أَقُولُ لِأَبِي وَأُمِّي إِذَا قَالَا لِي مِنْ أَيْنَ جَاءَتْكِ هَذِهِ الْبِنْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓarat ilayhi wa-ḥaqqaqathu fa-lammā ʿarafathu ghābat ʿan ṣawābihā wa-bakat wa-laṭamat wajhahā wa-qālat lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāhi qad waqaʿnā fī dhanbin ʿaẓīmin mādhā yakūnu al-ʿamalu wa-mā aqūlu li-abī wa-ummī idhā qālā lī min ayna jāʾatki hādhihi al-bintu
sentences.l: And she looked at him and made-certain of him; and when she knew him, she was absent from her right-mind, and wept and struck her face, and said: No might and no power but in God! We have fallen into a great sin; what shall the doing be? And what shall I say to my father and my mother when they say to me: From where has this girl come to you?
sentences.i: She looked at him and studied him, and when she knew him she lost her senses; she wept and struck her face, and said, “There is no might and no power but in God! We have fallen into a great sin. What is to be done? And what shall I say to my father and my mother, when they ask me, ‘Where did this girl come to you from?’”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ شَرْكَانُ الرَّأْيُ أَنْ أُزَوِّجَكِ بِالْحَاجِبِ وَأَدَعَكِ تُرَبِّي بِنْتِي عِنْدَهُ فِي بَيْتِهِ بِحَيْثُ لَايَعْلَمُ أَحَدٌ بِأَنَّكِ إِخْتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Sharkānu al-raʾyu an uzawwijaki bi-al-ḥājibi wa-adaʿaki tarabbī bintī ʿindahu fī baytihi bi-ḥaythu lā yaʿlamu aḥadun bi-annaki ikhtī
sentences.l: And Sharkān said: The opinion is that I marry-you-off to the chamberlain, and leave you to rear my daughter with him in his house, in such-a-way that no one knows that you are my sister.
sentences.i: Sharkān said, “The best course is for me to marry you to the chamberlain and leave you to bring up my daughter in his house, so that no one will know that you are my sister.”
sentences.n: The print puts a kasra on the alif of اختي; it is kept and vocalised as printed (ikhtī), the sense being the usual ukhtī, “my sister”.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا الَّذِي قَدَّرَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى عَلَيْنَا لَامَرَارَادَهُ فَمَا يَسْتُرُنَا إِلَّآ زَوَاجُكِ بِهَذَا الْحَاجِبِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَدْرِيَ أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā alladhī qaddarahu Allāhu taʿālā ʿalaynā lāmarārādahu fa-mā yasturunā illā zawājuki bi-hādhā al-ḥājibi qabla an yadriya aḥadun
sentences.l: And this is what God, exalted, has decreed upon us, lāmarārādahu; and nothing will cover us but your marriage to this chamberlain before anyone learns.
sentences.i: This is what God Most High has decreed for us — and there is no turning back from his will. Nothing will shelter us but your marriage to this chamberlain before anyone finds out.
sentences.n: The word لامراراده is garbled in the print. It is probably لا مردّ لإرادته, “there is no turning back of his will”, and is translated so; it is vocalised as one word, as printed. The edition also prints الآ with a long-alif mark for الا (illā).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَارَيَأْخُذُ بِخَاطِرِهَا وَيُقَبِّلُ رَأْسَهَا فَقَالَتْ لَهُ وَمَا تُسَمَّى الْبِنْتُ قَالَ تُسَمِّيهَا قُضِىَ فَكَانَ
sentences.tr: thumma ṣāra yaʾkhudhu bi-khāṭirihā wa-yuqabbilu raʾsahā fa-qālat lahu wa-mā tusammā al-bintu qāla tusammīhā quḍiya fa-kāna
sentences.l: Then he began taking-with her heart and kissing her head; and she said to him: And what is the girl called? He said: Call her “It-was-decreed, and so it was.”
sentences.i: Then he began to soothe her and to kiss her head. She said to him, “And what is the girl to be called?” He said, “Call her Quḍiya-fa-kān.”
sentences.n: قُضِيَ فَكَانَ, “it was decreed, and so it came to be”, is the girl's name; in the tale she is also known as Quḍiya Fakān. The idiom أَخَذَ بِخَاطِرِهِ means “to comfort, to humour someone”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ زَوَّجَهَا لِلْحَاجِبِ الْكَبِيرِ وَنَقَلَهَا إِلَى بَيْتِهِ هِيَ وَبِنْتَهَا فَرَبَّوْهَا عَلَى أَكْتَافِ الْجَوَارِي وَوَاظَبُوا عَلَيْهَا بِالْأَشْرِبَهِ وَأَنْوَاعِ السُّفُوفِ
sentences.tr: thumma zawwajahā li-al-ḥājibi al-kabīri wa-naqalahā ilā baytihi hiya wa-bintahā fa-rabbawhā ʿalā aktāfi al-jawārī wa-wāẓabū ʿalayhā bi-al-ashribati wa-anwāʿi al-sufūfi
sentences.l: Then he married her to the great chamberlain, and he moved her to his house, she and her daughter; and they reared her upon the shoulders of the slave-girls, and persevered with her with the drinks and kinds-of the powders.
sentences.i: Then he married her to the chief chamberlain, who took her to his house, she and her daughter; and the slave-girls carried the child on their shoulders and reared her, and kept on giving her syrups and every kind of medicinal powder.
sentences.n: The print has الاشربه with final ه for ة (al-ashriba), a common Middle Arabic spelling; vocalised as the standard form.

sentences.t: هَذَا كُلُّهُ وَأَخُوهَا ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ مَعَ الْوَقَّادِ بِدِمَشْقَ
sentences.tr: hādhā kulluhu wa-akhūhā Ḍawʾu al-makāni maʿa al-waqqādi bi-Dimashqa
sentences.l: All this, and her brother Light-of-the-place with the stoker in Damascus.
sentences.i: All this while her brother, Ḍawʾ al-Makān, was with the stoker in Damascus.
sentences.n: Ḍawʾ al-Makān, “Light of the Place”, is Nuzhat al-Zamān's brother, left ill in Jerusalem and now in Damascus with the bath-stoker who took him in.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَ يَوْمًا مِنَ الْأَيَّامِ أَقْبَلَ بَرِيدٌ مِنْ عِنْدِ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ شَرْكَانَ وَمَعَهُ كِتَابٌ فَأَخَذَهُ وَقَرَأَهُ وَإِذَا فِيهِ بَعْدَ الْبَسْمَلَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kāna yawman min al-ayyāmi aqbala barīdun min ʿindi al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni ilā al-maliki Sharkāna wa-maʿahu kitābun fa-akhadhahu wa-qaraʾahu wa-idhā fīhi baʿda al-basmalati
sentences.l: And when it was a day of the days, a courier came from the presence of the king ʿUmar son-of al-Nuʿmān to the king Sharkān, and with him a letter; and he took it and read it, and behold, in it, after the basmala:
sentences.i: One day a courier arrived from King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, bringing a letter for King Sharkān. He took it and read it, and found in it, after the invocation of God's name:
sentences.n: The basmala is the opening formula “In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate”.

sentences.t: اعْلَمْ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ الْعَزِيزُ أَنِّي حَزِينٌ حُزْنًا شَدِيدًا عَلَي فِرَاقِ الْأَوْلَادِ وَعَدِمْتُ الرُّقَادَ وَلَا زَمَنِى السُّهَادُ
sentences.tr: iʿlam ayyuhā al-maliku al-ʿazīzu annī ḥazīnun ḥuznan shadīdan ʿalā firāqi al-awlādi wa-ʿadimtu al-ruqāda wa-lāzamanī al-suhādu
sentences.l: Know, O king the dear, that I am sorrowful, with a severe sorrow, over the parting of the children, and I have lacked sleep, and wakefulness has clung-to me.
sentences.i: Know, dear king, that I am deeply grieved at the parting from my children. I have lost my sleep and wakefulness has become my companion.
sentences.n: ولا زمنى is printed with a space; it is read as ولازمني. Sleep (الرقاد) and wakefulness (السهاد) make a rhyming pair, as is usual in letters.

sentences.t: وَقَدْأَرْ سَلْتُ هَذَا الْكِتَابَ إِلَيْكَ فَصْلَ وُصُولِ هَذَا الْكِتَابِ تُجَهِّزْ لَنَا الْمَالَ وَالْخَرَاجَ وَتُرْسِلْ صُحْبَتَهُ الْجَارِيَةَ الَّتِي اشْتَرَيْتَهَا وَتَزَوَّجْتَ بِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qad arsaltu hādhā al-kitāba ilayka faṣla wuṣūli hādhā al-kitābi tujahhiz lanā al-māla wa-al-kharāja wa-tursil ṣuḥbatahu al-jāriyata allatī ishtaraytahā wa-tazawwajta bihā
sentences.l: And I have sent this letter to you; the cutting-off-of the arrival-of this letter, prepare for us the money and the tribute, and send in its company the girl whom you bought and married.
sentences.i: I have sent you this letter: the moment it reaches you, make ready the money and the tribute for us, and send with it the girl whom you bought and married.
sentences.n: فصل is the print's word; it is read as the adverbial “at the moment of”, possibly a slip for a more usual فور or عند. تجهز and ترسل are jussive-looking imperatives with the final vowel dropped, as printed.

sentences.t: فَإِنِّي أَحْبَبْتُ أَنْ أَرَاهَا وَأَسْمَعَ كَلَامَهَا لِأَنَّهُ جَاءَنَا مِنْ بِلَادِ الرُّومِ عَجُوزٌ مِنَ الصَّالِحَاتِ وَصُحْبَتَهَا خَمْسُ جَوَارٍ نُهَّدٌ أَبْكَارٌ وَمَدٌّ حَازُوا مِنَ الْعِلْمِ وَالْأَدَبِ وَفُنُونِ الْحِكْمَةِ مَا يَجِبُ عَلَى الْإِنْسَانِ مَعْرِفَتُهُ وَيَعْجِزُ عَنْ وَصْفِ هَذِهِ الْعَجُوزِوَ مَنْ مَعَهَا اللِّسَانُ
sentences.tr: fa-innī aḥbabtu an arāhā wa-asmaʿa kalāmahā li-annahu jāʾanā min bilādi al-Rūmi ʿajūzun min al-ṣāliḥāti wa-ṣuḥbatahā khamsu jawārin nuhhadun abkārun wa-madd ḥāzū min al-ʿilmi wa-al-adabi wa-funūni al-ḥikmati mā yajibu ʿalā al-insāni maʿrifatuhu wa-yaʿjizu ʿan waṣfi hādhihi al-ʿajūzi wa-man maʿahā al-lisānu
sentences.l: For I wished to see her and hear her speech, because there came to us from the lands of Rome an old woman, of the righteous women, and in her company five girls, full-breasted, virgins, and madd, who had gained of knowledge and letters and the arts of wisdom what is-obligatory upon a person, his knowing; and the tongue is unable to describe this old woman and those with her.
sentences.i: For I wished to see her and to hear her speak. There has come to us from the lands of Rome an old woman, one of the pious, and with her five young women, full-breasted virgins, who have gained such knowledge, letters and the arts of wisdom as a man ought to know; the tongue is helpless to describe this old woman and those with her.
sentences.n: The word printed ومد (after أبكار) is obscure and may be corrupt, or a word has dropped out; it is vocalised as a bare noun and left out of the idiomatic English. بلاد الروم, “the lands of Rome”, is Byzantium/Anatolia. The print runs العجوز and و together (al-ʿajūzi wa-).

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُنَّ حُزْنَ أَنْوَاعَ الْعِلْمِ وَالْفَضِيلَةِ وَالْحِكْمَةِ فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُهُنَّ أَحْبَبْتُهُنَّ وَقَدِ اشْتَهَيْتُ أَنْ يَكُنَّ فِي قَصْرِي وَفِي مِلْكِ يَدِي لِأَنَّهُنَّ لَمْ يُوجَدْ لَهُنَّ نَظِيرٌ عِنْدَ سَائِرِ الْمُلُوكِ
sentences.tr: fa-innahunna ḥuzna anwāʿa al-ʿilmi wa-al-faḍīlati wa-al-ḥikmati fa-lammā raʾaytuhunna aḥbabtuhunna wa-qadi ishtahaytu an yakunna fī qaṣrī wa-fī milki yadī li-annahunna lam yūjad lahunna naẓīrun ʿinda sāʾiri al-mulūki
sentences.l: For they have gained kinds-of knowledge and virtue and wisdom; and when I saw them I loved them, and I desired that they be in my palace and in the possession-of my hand, because there was not found for them a like among the rest of the kings.
sentences.i: For they have mastered every kind of knowledge, virtue and wisdom. When I saw them I loved them, and I longed to have them in my palace, in my own possession, for no other king has anything like them.

sentences.t: فَسَأَلْتُ الْمَرْأَةَ الْعَجُوزَ عَنْ ثَمَنِهِنَّ فَقَالَتْ لَا أَبِيعُهُنَّ إِلَّابِخَرَاجِ دِمَشْقَ وَأَنَا وَاللَّهِ مَا رَأَيْتُ هَذَا كَثِيرًا فِي ثَمَنِهِنَّ فَإِنَّ الْوَاحِدَةَ مِنْهُنَّ تُسَاوِى الثَّمَنَ جَمِيعَهُ فَأَجَبْتُهَا إِلَى ذَلِكَ وَدَخَلْتُ بِهِنَّ إِلَى قَصْرِي وَبَقِينَ فِي حَوْزِي
sentences.tr: fa-saʾaltu al-marʾata al-ʿajūza ʿan thamanihinna fa-qālat lā abīʿuhunna illā bi-kharāji Dimashqa wa-anā wa-allāhi mā raʾaytu hādhā kathīran fī thamanihinna fa-inna al-wāḥidata minhunna tusāwī al-thamana jamīʿahu fa-ajabtuhā ilā dhālika wa-dakhaltu bihinna ilā qaṣrī wa-baqīna fī ḥawzī
sentences.l: And I asked the woman, the old one, about their price, and she said: I do not sell them except for the tribute of Damascus. And I, by God, did not see this as much for their price, for one of them is worth the whole price; so I answered her to that, and entered with them into my palace, and they remained in my possession.
sentences.i: I asked the old woman their price, and she said, “I will sell them only for the tribute of Damascus.” By God, I did not think that too much for them, for any one of them is worth the whole of it. So I agreed, and took them into my palace, and they remain in my keeping.
sentences.n: The print runs الا and بخراج together (illā bi-kharāji). The tribute of Damascus is the revenue of Sharkān's province, which his father Nuʿmān had made over to him.

sentences.t: فَعَجِّلْ لَنَا بِالْخَرَاجِ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ تُسَافِرَ الْمَرْأَةُ إِلَى بِلَادِهَا وَأَرْسِلْ إِلَيْنَا الْجَارِيَةَ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ تُنَاظِرَ هُنَّ بَيْنَ الْعُلَمَاءِ فَإِذَا غَلَبَتْهُنَّ أَرْسَلْتُهَا لَكَ وَصُحْبَتَهَا خَرَاجُ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿajjil lanā bi-al-kharāji li-ajli an tusāfira al-marʾatu ilā bilādihā wa-arsil ilaynā al-jāriyata li-ajli an tunāẓirahunna bayna al-ʿulamāʾi fa-idhā ghalabathunna arsaltuhā laka wa-ṣuḥbatahā kharāju Baghdāda
sentences.l: So hasten for us with the tribute, for the sake that the woman may travel to her lands; and send to us the girl, for the sake that she may dispute them among the learned; and if she overcomes them, I shall send her to you, and in her company the tribute of Baghdad.
sentences.i: So hurry the tribute to us, so that the woman may travel back to her own country, and send the girl to us, so that she may debate them before the scholars. If she defeats them, I shall send her back to you, and with her the tribute of Baghdad.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُ—بَ—احِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech the permitted.
sentences.i: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech unspoken.
sentences.n: The stock close of a night. The print's last word is damaged (الم—ب—اح, with dashes inside it); it is read as the formula's usual al-mubāḥ.
